Five European teams to watch as Mauricio Pochettino begins Manchester United era

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the international break is over, and it's now time to get back to the usual business with European soccer resuming alongside the MLS playoffs in the United States.
  • Sources indicate that the biggest change of the break: Manchester United sacked coach and club legend Michael Carrick and replaced him with Pochettino, who makes his Premier League comeback after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea.
  • In a recent development, speaking of a former Manchester United head coach, Jose Mourinho has had some ups and downs early in his first season back at Real Madrid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the international break is over, and it's now time to get back to the usual business with European soccer resuming alongside the MLS playoffs in the United States. It was supposed to be a quiet break, but that wasn't the case at all, since Manchester United decided to part ways with Michael Carrick and appointed Mauricio Pochettino, who had recently signed a new deal with the United States men's national team but decided to leave after the break. Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid will battle with Barcelona for the LaLiga title, while Como are still one of the most interesting sides to watch in the near future. Let's now take a look at the five teams to watch after the break, starting with the Red Devils.

Sources indicate that the biggest change of the break: Manchester United sacked coach and club legend Michael Carrick and replaced him with Pochettino, who makes his Premier League comeback after coaching Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea. As the English giants are currently sitting 18th in the standings, this is a major task for the now-former USMNT head coach, who will make his return at Anfield against Liverpool in his opening game at United. It's a daunting start in one of the most hostile atmospheres in the country. For Pochettino, the challenge will be to strike the right balance between delivering short-term results and laying the foundations for a latest chapter at the club. His ambition will be to usher in a fresh cycle at an institution that has endured one crisis after another since Sir Alex Ferguson stepped down more than a decade ago.

In a recent development, speaking of a former Manchester United head coach, Jose Mourinho has had some ups and downs early in his first season back at Real Madrid. After winning an exciting away El Clasico match against Barcelona, Mourinho's team is only three points behind Hansi Flick's side right now and is eyeing the possibility of challenging them for the LaLiga title this season. They certainly have all the ingredients to make it happen, particularly following some remarkable additions to the squad in the summer of 2026. Kylian Mbappe and Jude Bellingham are arguably entering their prime and appear ready to take the team to the next level, supported by a number of exciting young prospects who could play a key role in shaping the club's future. Will Mourinho be able to win a trophy in his first season back at the club? That would be a story.

If there is one team to watch in Serie A, it's Como. The side led by Cesc Fabregas is impressing both domestically and in Europe, as it is right now fourth in the league-phase standings of the UEFA Champions League. Fabregas can count on some of the best players in the league, such as Nico Paz, the Argentine talent who is now also expected to lead the national team after Lionel Messi's retirement. The question is how far Como can go this season, given that playing every three days can be a substantial challenge for players who have never experienced it. They may still have to pay the price in the league, but qualifying for at least the playoffs of Europe's elite competition would remain a realistic target and, given the circumstances, a remarkable achievement in itself.

It's always about Manchester City: the Citizens are still waiting to learn what sanctions they will face after an independent commission found them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules. They are facing a challenging season that might have an impact on the years ahead. It's not clear what the sanctions will be, but we will likely know more before the end of the current season. On the pitch, they are also facing a season of changes as longtime coach Pep Guardiola left the club in the summer and was replaced by Enzo Maresca, who is now overseeing that transition.

Spanish soccer is not just about Real Madrid and Barcelona: Atletico Madrid are once again near the top of the standings, five points behind the Blaugrana. Diego Simeone, who has coached the club since 2011, is an Atletico Madrid legend who has faced so many changes over the years but has always been able to recreate the right atmosphere and environment to succeed. Atletico have changed their tactical approach and playing style many times, but they are still near the top, and that is what makes Simeone special.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists should resist political pressure to provide certainty when the evidence suggests otherwise, says Andy Stirling.Your browser does not support the audio element.Download MP3See transcript.

Science’s greatest failure is not getting things wrong, but by sometimes pretending that there is more certainty than there really is, says social scientist Andy Stirling.

This can happen, he states, when researchers face political pressure to provide a single, definitive answer, when the evidence is far more complex.

In the final episode of a six-part podcast series about failure in science, Stirling, an emeritus professor at the University of Sussex in Brighton, UK, draws on examples from climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, environmental campaigns and energy policy.

“In those areas, science just does not convey the degree of uncertainty and of variability and of how many potentially viable options are being cut out when you just give one clear answer,” he says. “It thinks it’s helping society by just giving one picture of the truth. And in fact, it’s undermining both itself and democracy when it does that.”.

Stirling, whose research includes science and technology policy and environmental politics, says that on occasions politicians have almost literally hidden behind scientists on a podium, who have relied on their authority and expertise to protect them.

Recent findings suggest that earlier this year, Stirling spoke at a one-day conference on failure in science, with a focus on careers and innovation. It was held at Imperial College London in partnership with Nature.

One thing that got me going with all this was in back in the ’90 s I was looking at risk assessments, cost-benefit analysis, life cycle assessments.

All these highly technical quantitative assessments in the energy sector.

Industry observers note that cutting a long story short, they were, the energy sector was the place where these things were developed to their most mature, sophisticated form. And if you looked at any given study, you got this really confident idea.

This is what the risks of nuclear are compared to renewables, compared to gas, or whatever it is.

The same with the other methods I mentioned.

And then every single time you stand back and you look at the literature as a whole, not just peer-reviewed literature, but the literature embodied in law.

So the most kind of authoritatively treated source of data on these things, and you found you could get any answer you like across that peer-reviewed literature.

It depends on the framing. The models give you an answer that depends on how you frame the question.

And that for me kind of radicalized me because I realized that none of the committees, none of the reports around the world were fully representing what the literature they were consulting told us, that you can get all kinds of different answers.

And what matters is not just the one answer, the risk, the cost, environmental costs, the ecosystem service.

What matters is how that changes depending on assumptions, that’s how science should speak to policy, but also to society, telling us how these things depend.

The reason I said that, a lot of people talk about lamenting the fact we have policy-based evidence rather than evidence-based policy, and it’s a good point.

You know, you get all kinds of practices making things up all the time, all over the place in every sector.

But my point wasn’t to lambast that. It wasn’t to say, to lament yet again "you guys are just stitching it up." It was to say "Actually, I’ve never yet seen an area where the evidence compels a single policy.".

So even when you do get the best quality evidence, it is never without uncertainties. It’s never without differences of implication for action, depending on which discipline was actually most influential, how the questions were asked, what the baselines were, etc. etc.

So I have yet to see any body of analysis based on evidence that compels a single decision.

So when you hear people talking about evidence-based policy as if there were only one policy that could have been based on the evidence, they’re basically again being post-truth.

They’re (to be a bit more colourful about it, they’re telling porkies.".

Because there will always be values, interests, assumptions at work, and it’s not a bad thing. It’s inevitable.

Industry observers note that that’s how science, you know, depends. For instance, on BSE whether vets or were the epidemiologists in charge? He got a very different answer.

And in COVID, you know, again, we-I mean, it’s still too early to say, as Mao stated, I think about the French Revolution, was it? But it’s too early to say.

But you can still see that what was the best way to act on the available evidence, economic as well as epidemiological, and the different ways of interpreting the epidemiological evidence.

It’s very clear now that it’s not so clear-cut what a particular country should do.

It has been revealed that different countries do different things. There are different ways of looking back on it, looking at the time and seeing what was good and what was bad.

So, without taking position on either side, it’s far from clear that there was a single definitive action that should have been taken.

Sources indicate that I defy anyone to actually come back and defend that. There’ll be a matter of judgment as between really quite radically different policies.

So COVID is an example of this. I think we had to pretend there was one policy because it was so stressful.

Politicians had to pretend because otherwise they would have to hide behind their chief scientists, literally sometimes, literally behind them on the podium, hiding behind them because they needed that authority to protect them from the inevitable uncertainties that everyone believed were really there, even though they weren’t acknowledging it in the graphs.

I mean, blame management, trust, public acceptance.

These things are the most vital commodities in politics. So yeah, and it’s you know apocryphally, people have all kinds of anecdotes out on these advisory committees.

I’ve served a little bit on some of them. You know, the number of times in which the politicians will intimate, "I won’t hesitate to hide behind you," almost as a joke.

But so you know, scientists respond to that in different ways. But by and large, they think, "Well, okay, we’ve got to be responsible. Let’s give these guys a single prescriptive answer, even though we know among ourselves that we could have got a different answer, but we’ve got a responsibility not to do an to do to do an elevator pitch.".

It has been revealed that you know, not to give on the one hand, on the other, as Margaret Thatcher mentioned, "Save me from the two-handed economist. I want a one-handed economist.".

Industry observers note that she wants it because of justification, but actually, it’s a responsibility of the economist, or in this case, a scientist, to actually explain how it does depend. It always does depend.

If they don’t explain that, then they are failing, I would say science, and failing society, failing democracy.

Other things are really complicated. there’s a lot of real challenges. I don’t want to pretend it’s easier than it really is.

Recent findings suggest that but actually, we shouldn’t be paralyzed by this. Look at science itself. When it developed in the 17th century, motto of the Royal Society, nullius in verba, that was basically saying that principles of accountability, of argument, of deliberation really mattered, of treating people more equally than many institutions do. That’s not the opposite of democracy. That is democracy.

Science was about, in many ways, democratizing knowledge.

According to recent reports, you know, you needed to argue, you need to show evidence and do analyzes in rigorous ways. But it should be open to anyone to do that, and to any perspective, no matter how ridiculous it sounds, if it can substantiate itself.

So science and democracy are not on opposite sides.

So I think, rather than counterpointing them, like science is against democracy, we can’t trust democracy, going to undermine science, actually, see it the other way round: that science is an embodiment of democracy.

It’s when it is at its best. It’s when it’s being democratic about the ability to challenge power inside science, and that’s how we solve the problems of science.

It’s also how we solve the problems at the moment of democracy, which science is, sadly, because it’s forced to be more authoritarian in pretending a singular truth.

It’s forced into that not by democracy, but by power that is also eroding democracy.

So I think the answer is democracy.

Science, when it comes to advise policymakers, yes, please do your best, but don’t think of yourself just giving a single expedient answer so that a politician goes away happy and can act without worrying about blame.

Inform society at large about the assumptions that went into that.

Show how it depends, and if you do that, you’re informing democracy as much as the powerful actors who are, you know, maybe conferring the patronage on the scientists.

Science fails when it’s not being plural enough.

It needs to be plural about who’s involved, about the questions that are asked, about the disciplines that get around the table, about how it conveys its interpretations of its understandings out to society, and it needs to just not be scared of representing that plurality because with that comes the conditions.

It has been revealed that it’s not just anything goes. It’s not plural for plurality’s sake.

It’s then saying under what conditions you get answer X or answer Y, and that’s more scientific.

It’s more rigorous to behave in that way.

According to recent reports, when science does that, it’s being more scientific when it’s plural. So I think science fails most when it reduces all those kinds of plurality.

To just a singular idea of truth.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In recent years, Louisville City FC have been one of the most successful regular-season teams in United Soccer League history, but it hasn't translated to winning the significant game. They haven't won the USL Championship since 2018, and while this season has been a trying time dealing with injuries and a latest coach taking over, they're playing their best soccer when it matters to set up a strange clash with Sacramento Republic at noon Eastern on Saturday. What's strange isn't that it's Louisville and Sacramento meeting, but that the match kicks off at 9 a.m. local time, a time Louisville forward Ray Serrano notes he hasn't played soccer at since he was 15. While it's a regular training time for Louisville and they'll try to keep things on an East Coast timeline, it's hard not to take the shift into account when planning for a final.

It's a challenge that comes with the desire to reach as many fans as possible with a final of this magnitude. Leagues have to work with broadcast networks to ensure that the slots work, and for the USL, having the game on CBS is worth the risk of a 9 a.m. local start with a West Coast team hosting. It's nothing Louisville won't be prepared for, as they look to keep their internal clocks on Eastern Standard Time.

Industry observers note that "No, we're trying to stay on Eastern Time, so for us, it's training time," defender Kyle Adams said. "Wake up at 8:00 a.m., but really it's 5:00 a.m. Go to sleep a little bit earlier. Try to do everything really just to stay on Eastern Time, eat a little bit earlier on the night before, and just treat it as going into training, and then get after them.".

Other teams have dealt with similar issues, like the Los Angeles Rams when playing an NFL game in Australia, but it's still a struggle to deal with en route to a cup final as Louisville look to reach the pinnacle of the sport for the first time since 2018. Winners of the Prinx Tires USL Cup during the regular season, they do have cup experience that will prove to be fruitful in this competition, which Adams noted has been something that brings the injury-riddled squad together. "We know in the last few years we've struggled in these knockout games, but this year we've turned it on," Serrano remarked. "It has been really good preparation, just the mentality of going into them, how we deal with the pressure, and we're seeing the fruits of all that now.".

It's cliche to say that because of the adversity that they've dealt with, the club is playing its best soccer when it matters, but between using four goalkeepers during the season and seeing manager Danny Cruz depart to be an assistant manager with Minnesota United, it hasn't been an easy task for interim manager Simon Bird to get this team on the right track at this critical juncture.

Recent findings suggest that "Going back to the main part is the adversity that we've faced. You mentioned injuries, having to deal with that side of it, some of the various parts of the season, different things we've had to deal with from a tactical or technical standpoint, where we've lost games, and we feel that we shouldn't have lost games," Bird said when reflecting on the team's development under his leadership. "The most impressive thing I said to the guys today, yesterday in training, we worked on our defensive structure, but the whole training session I thought was excellent, not just the defensive side, off the ball but with the ball, and to see it all come together towards the end of the season is really rewarding. Hopefully, we can carry that on and put together a complete performance, and that's what we've had throughout the season-moments where we've let ourselves down in all these different areas, set pieces, maybe transition at other times, in front of goal. So, putting it all together for a complete performance on Saturday is the goal.".

Traveling away to a tough environment in Heart Health Park, Louisville will meet the hottest team in the league in Sacramento Republic. They've ridden a club-record 16-game unbeaten run to the final based on their defense. That has set a strong foundation to build on, and it could make the final one where the first team to score a goal wins the match. Sacramento's squad also has experience in USL Cup finals, which goes a long way when preparing for games of this stature.

"I don't think it can hurt to have that. This would be a step forward for my first final. I think experience is invaluable for players and for staff," Sacramento coach Neil Collins remarked. "But then there's also the recognition that every game is different, every team is different, and every season is different. So it's just trying to get the balance right and enjoy the opportunity. You've got to have the mechanisms to control the things you can control. Obviously, the opposition team is trying to do the same, and we've got to do everything we can to be ready to take the opportunity when it comes. But the experience will definitely help us; there's plenty of that in our dressing room.".

It has been revealed that it's a final where the best that the league has to offer will be on display, and it couldn't come at a better time. The summer of soccer, with the United States hosting the World Cup alongside Mexico and Canada, has truly turned into a soccer avalanche, and this final showcases one of the top atmospheres in the league. You can't ask for much better than that, as no matter what, a drought will come to an end. Sacramento Republic haven't won the final since 2014, while Louisville haven't won since 2018, and for these clubs, it will mean a lot to get back to the top.

Why Manchester United will surpass Liverpool’s title drought

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “My greatest challenge was knocking Liverpool right off their f****** perch.”.
  • Sir Alex Ferguson’s famous quote has become so embedded in football folklore that its provenance is often misremembered.
  • Industry observers note that the then-Manchester United manager did not deliver the emphatic line in the early years of his tenure, as is sometimes claimed, but during a poor run of form in September 2002.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“My greatest challenge was knocking Liverpool right off their f****** perch.”.

Sir Alex Ferguson’s famous quote has become so embedded in football folklore that its provenance is often misremembered.

Industry observers note that the then-Manchester United manager did not deliver the emphatic line in the early years of his tenure, as is sometimes claimed, but during a poor run of form in September 2002. The Red Devils had won seven of the previous 10 Premier League crowns, while Liverpool were not even halfway through their 30-year title drought.

Ferguson uttered that comment during Liverpool’s 13th successive campaign without winning the top flight. Fast forward almost a quarter of a century, and United are 13 years into a decline that set in as soon as the Scot retired.

It has been revealed that the Red Devils’ title drought is already nearly half as long as the one Liverpool experienced between 1990 and 2020. They are in the Premier League relegation zone ahead of today’s trip to Anfield, so we can safely say their wait will stretch to at least the 2027/28 season, which will be 15 years since they last won the top flight.

Sources indicate that clearly, the 30-year mark is still a long way off and plenty can happen in that time. But it is also undeniable that United are as far from title challengers as they have been since 2013 and there are no signs of that changing.

That starts from the top. In September, executive co-chairman Avram Glazer told Deutsche Bank’s Sports Investment Conference in London that clubs of United’s stature are not dependent on success on the pitch for commercial power. The quotes, first reported by The Athletic, emerged this month when the Red Devils were about to sack manager Michael Carrick following their slide down the table.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Glazer’s comments were strikingly similar to those of former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward in May 2018, when he told shareholders: “Playing performance doesn’t really have a meaningful impact on what we can do on the commercial side of the business.”.

The fact that those two quotes occurred eight-and-a-half years apart suggests that as long as the Glazer family remain United’s majority owners, the club will prioritise commercial gain over on-pitch success.

The Americans also appear to be in no rush to sell their majority stake in the club, despite being universally unpopular with the fanbase. A report from TEAMtalk last week claimed they are unlikely to step away until United’s proposed 100,000-capacity stadium is built - which may not be until 2035 - in order to extract maximum value from their investment.

Other outlets claim the Glazers could be interested in selling their stake to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe before then, but that certainly would not guarantee success, with the British businessman’s record in football across United, French club Nice and Swiss outfit Lausanne-Sport patchy at best.

When Ratcliffe bought a minority stake in the club in February 2024, taking control of sporting operations, it was supposed to end a decade of managerial mis-steps and overpaying for underperforming players.

However, the situation has deteriorated further, with chief executive officer Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox facing heavy criticism from fans. The Red Devils finished 15th in 2024/25 and have won just one league game this term, while the one positive half-season of the Ratcliffe era came when Carrick took over as interim boss from Ruben Amorim - another failed appointment - in January and overperformed expectations by qualifying for the Champions League.

Ultimately, United will not become a force again without an ownership change. As the Manchester United Supporters Trust (MUST) said in its statement following Carrick’s sacking: “Another change of head coach cannot repair what the ownership continues to undermine.”.

This is where Liverpool’s title drought is instructive. Part of the reason for the Reds’ decline in the 1990s and 2000s was because they were overtaken financially by their rivals - initially Ferguson’s United, then Chelsea following Roman Abramovich’s takeover - under their long-time owners, the Moores family.

Recent findings suggest that after the chaotic ownership of Tom Hicks and George Gillett, Fenway Sports Group (FSG) bought Liverpool in 2010. FSG did not get it right immediately, but after appointing Jurgen Klopp as manager in 2015 and putting the right people in key positions, such as sporting director Michael Edwards, the Reds were able to challenge regularly for the biggest honours again.

The team that won the title in 2020 featured some big-money recruits, most notably Virgil van Dijk and Alisson, but also several cheaper signings that resulted from a recruitment overhaul, such as Mo Salah, Roberto Firmino and Andy Robertson.

But the key point is that it took Liverpool 10 years of FSG ownership to end their title drought, and only once every department at the club, from the owners to the recruitment team to Klopp, were aligned in pursuit of on-pitch success.

It is why new United manager Mauricio Pochettino can only do so much. Like Carrick last season, Erik ten Hag in 2022/23 or Ole Gunnar Solskjaer in 2020/21, there may well be good spells during his tenure, but to paraphrase MUST, the head coach at Old Trafford will inevitably be undermined by the owners sooner or later.

It has been revealed that even when the Glazers eventually sell, we cannot expect the club to immediately become the force they once were, as the Liverpool example indicates. It takes time to return to the top when you have been also-rans for so long.

In a recent development, that is why it is easy to see how United’s title drought could stretch beyond 30 years, as hypothetical as that sounds right now. If the Glazers stay in charge for the foreseeable future, the upcoming owners would need time to undo the damage and put everything in place for success. Only then could United start to consistently challenge for the title and there is no guarantee they would win it straight away.

This scenario would have seemed unthinkable when Ferguson made his famous quip in 2002, but when you fall off your perch it is difficult to get back up - as Liverpool know all too well.

Industry News: 'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin: Europe remains committed to Ukraine

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19).
  • In a recent development, extensive security measures have already been confirmed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants.
  • Industry observers note that the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: Around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter.

In a recent development, extensive security measures have already been confirmed for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets.

Industry observers note that the "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Industry observers note that led by Germany, France and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London.

Recent findings suggest that but what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic.

Industry observers note that "The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal," he told DW. "There is no proposal outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises.".

Nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward.

Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice.

This has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)?

Sources indicate that after the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, Merz stated: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear.".

Industry observers note that but what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President Antonio Costa, would also take part.

Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate says a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under.

In a recent development, "Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations," Meister remarked. "Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that.".

German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator.

Recent findings suggest that at the federal government's regular press briefing, he remarked: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, struck a rather different tone last week.

Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he stated: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations.".

Government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question.".

Hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: Peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about.

In a recent development, european supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the concern is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly.

In a recent development, according to the latest DeutschlandTrend survey on the glitch, conducted or German public broadcaster ARD in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war.

Recent findings suggest that A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing matter in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine.

This article was originally written in German.

#117174. Industry News: NWSL, U.S. Soccer continue focus on women's soccer growth with player and executive development programs

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2007 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Cbssports ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: NWSL, U.S. Soccer continue focus on women's soccer growth with player and executive development programs

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that WASHINGTON, D.C.
  • In the first of four announcements she teased was in service of that.
  • The NWSL's newly introduced initiatives reflect a shifting focus across the American soccer landscape, one that seems driven by the heightened interest in the sport courtesy of this year's World Cup in North America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that WASHINGTON, D.C. – The NWSL has always been a measuring stick for the growth of women's soccer in the U.S., which in recent years has been headlined by skyrocketing expansion fees and increased fan engagement. There's a buzzword that continues to pop up around the league, one that is rarely associated with the key performance indicators – pipeline. After she read out another list of attendance figures and viewership numbers before the 2026 season wraps up with Saturday's NWSL Championship (8 p.m. ET, CBS, Paramount+), commissioner Jessica Berman made a hard pivot in her state of the league remarks on Thursday to say the league is officially in the business of prioritizing said pipeline.

In the first of four announcements she teased was in service of that. The NWSL announced two initiatives on Thursday: the creation of a player development rule (PDR) and a sporting executive leadership program, designed specifically to focus on the foundation of the league's structure. The plans are a marriage of the league's business model and sporting objectives, a tacit understanding that the two go hand-in-hand, especially for a league that is admittedly driven by star power. These newly introduced plans, though, are hardly the only initiatives that will influence the pipeline.

The NWSL's newly introduced initiatives reflect a shifting focus across the American soccer landscape, one that seems driven by the heightened interest in the sport courtesy of this year's World Cup in North America. The league's financial stability enabled this shift but beyond that, there are overlapping commitments across the industry to finally fix one of American soccer's most evident problems – the pipeline. The sport's success in this country has often come in spite of a fractured youth soccer system, one that U.S. Soccer hopes to unite in the coming years.

The parties, be it in conjunction or individually, are also dead set on ensuring the women's game is held in equal regard to the men's every step of the way.

The PDR joins a list of NWSL rules in recent years that have incentivized clubs to recruit young players more easily such as the U-18 Entry Mechanism and organizing its first-ever combine last year. The new rule requires participating clubs to develop a curriculum that supports player development and is tied directly to salary cap relief.

"What can we do at the league to motivate and incentivize clubs to develop players?" Sarah Gregorius, the NWSL's vice president of sporting, told CBS Sports. "What do we have in our toolkit? And one of the things we obviously have in our toolkit is a salary cap and we can use that as a motivation and as an incentive to encourage the types of behavior around player development that we want to see, and hopefully, it's really our first structural foray into player development. Again, it's deliberately an incentive. It's not a mandate. It's up to the clubs. If they want to participate, if they want to access the reward, they know what they have to do in order to do that.".

There is a perceived industry standard about developing young players, even if it is as far from an exact science as it gets. Academy systems tied to clubs are how players often come up the ranks – that is true across the men's game including in MLS and increasingly so for women's players in Europe. The NWSL does not have a streamlined system that mirrors the academy set-up and interestingly enough, is not actually trying to go in that direction.

Industry observers note that "This is a pretty unique country," Gregorius said. "It doesn't actually work to pick something up from overseas and plop it down over here and I'm actually not convinced in the two years that I've spent here and everything that I've learned that this vertical academy system across the clubs makes the most sense. There's already a ton of incredible player development happening. There's just a bit of a lack of cohesion and a lack of connection to the professional game … The Spanish model won't work here, the German model wouldn't work here, the Japanese model wouldn't work here. Got a ton of respect for what they're doing in their countries but the reason that it works is it's for those countries. We have to do something that works for this one, which has characteristics that no other country in the world has. F---, this place is significant. It's dynamic. There's a lot going on.".

Gregorius believes a league-issued mandate might further fracture an already splintered landscape.

Recent findings suggest that "If I think about it from a local level, some of our clubs are in markets that have thriving youth ecosystems, right?" Gregorius started. "So if all of a sudden there was a mandate from the league that every single club – which is what they do in England – has to come in and have a professional game academy, they're going to all of a sudden have to start pulling players out of those environments, which is disruptive for the kids. It's disruptive for the families. Some of those kids and families are also fans of the team. It's the icing on the cake in those particular markets so all of a sudden, you create tension. You create tension for the parents. You create tension for the kids. You create tension within the fan groups. They're like, 'Well, no, actually. You've stripped out my youth club in order to service a mandate from the league, not paying attention to the fact that all of your talented players have come through the system.' That's not what we want. That's bad for player development and it's bad for fan engagement, to be honest.".

Industry observers note that the NWSL is distinguishing itself from MLS, a league to which it has no formal ties but one that committed to the traditional academy system over a decade ago and can count it amongst its greatest successes. There's no stigma associated with the diverging path, though – U.S. Soccer has committed to viewing the women's game specifically through a female lens in recent years, an initiative championed by U.S. women's national team head coach Emma Hayes but embraced by many, either through her influence or separate from it.

"The intense focus on the pathway is very intentional," U.S. Soccer COO Dan Helfrich told CBS Sports. "The intense focus as we build the next version of the women and girls pathway, that it's done through a female lens, is very intentional and look, there is going to be, we believe, historic investment and interest in women's soccer and it's it's going to crescendo into the 2031 World Cup and making sure we take advantage of this moment to corral and direct the investment and interest in a sustainable way. I don't think there's anything that could have a greater legacy for women's soccer in our country than that.".

The distinction between the men's and women's games, even at the youth levels, is easy for Helfrich to make because they have always existed.

"The first thing is the environments for players to develop in," he mentioned. "it's really important that they're tailored to women and girl  and that includes environments for youth clubs and colleges and professional clubs and so some of the work, for example, of the Kang Women's Institute becomes really important to do the research to develop the insights and then for us to promulgate them into all these areas, that's different and if you look at the as-is state of the pathway, the league structures for girls are different than the league structures for boys. The role of college soccer for girls is different than the role of college soccer for boys and so practically, if you're trying to optimize a future, you apply a different lens.".

In a recent development, there's more shared consensus when it comes to developing leaders that will foster players' growth, which is where the sporting executive leadership program kicks in. The program is built around specialized education for sporting director types, the first yearlong edition of the initiative already in session. A cohort of six – Haley Carter of the Washington Spirit, Caitlin Carducci of the Orlando Pride, Angela Mangano of the Houston Dash, Jeff Agoos of the Portland Thorns, Kelly Cousins of the Utah Royals and Dome Guasch of the Boston Legacy – already took part in their first session of a project supported both by U.S. Soccer and FIFA.

"The 16, now 18, individuals who hold the highest sporting position at the clubs have an outsized impact on the on-field identity and on-field product of their club so therefore, all of those people have an an impact on the on-field product of the league," Gregorius noted. "It's also, curiously enough, one of the few roles within the sporting department that doesn't have a license. You don't need to have completed a particular license. There's no education requirements or anything like that so when we also did an audit of the 16 clubs and who was holding those positions, some have former players, some have lawyers, some have people with an operations background, some have people with a coaching background. It was very varied so we're like, okay, if we know that this group has a ton of impact, if we know that they don't go through any structured learning. Is there a way that we can wrap our arms around them and support them?".

The uniqueness of this program is that it is tied specifically to the NWSL, which operates independently of a men's league unlike some of its European counterparts or even the WNBA.

"It's the first of its kind because every other f---ing part of the world just cares about men's football so we're really, really proud of not only the commitment and the discipline around trying to get it off the ground," Gregorius mentioned.

It is in parallel with other initiatives the league and U.S. Soccer have worked on in recent years. The NWSL combine, for example, was also an effort to bolster female coaches while U.S. Soccer frequently uses its new national training center to conduct coaching courses with the youth game in mind.

"What I would say is to grow the game the way it needs to be grown, we can't underestimate or overlook the non-player part of development," Helfrich said, "and the non-player part of development is coaches. The non-player part of development is scouts. Non-player part of development is referees and the non-player part of development is front office, technical leaders and so, building a partnership with the NWSL on all of those important non-player development activities is a big priority.".

Sources indicate that the NWSL's partnership with U.S. Soccer on this program also speaks to a unique truth about American soccer. The women's game is held in incredibly high regard in the U.S. because of the historic success of the USWNT, who have four World Cup titles and five Olympic gold medals in their 40-year history. The USWNT's reputation of being serial winners is intrinsically tied to the health of the federation, the NWSL and in some ways, American soccer as a whole.

According to recent reports, "Honest to God, I've loved waking up every day and only thinking about the women's game," Gregorius, a former Upcoming Zealand international, said. "It's brilliant and it's very unique over here that we are able to do that and what I love about working with U.S. Soccer, as well, to be honest, is they're the same. They're almost more interested in the women's game sometimes than they are anything else … It's an organization that is already on the train, you know what I mean? The NWSL and our clubs, it's not even a question of being in the shadow of the men's game or any of that other bulls--- that you kind of encounter in other places. The focus is unwavering and that's brilliant.".

Recent findings suggest that manchester City surely cannot win the Champions League with a defence leaking goals and a goalkeeper making errors. But when Erling Haaland is in the team, anything seems possible.

This thrilling victory for City perfectly sums up their season: needless goals conceded, Gianluigi Donnarumma making a mistake, followed by Haaland saving the day with a winning goal.

In a recent development, “How can you stop Haaland?” read the headline in the local Volkszeitung newspaper on the morning of this Champions League clash. The answer is that it has been impossible for RB Leipzig.

Leipzig roll out the Red Bull carpet when they face the Norweigan. He has now scored 13 goals against them in nine matches, the most he has scored against a single team during his career. Industry observers note that good evening and welcome to live coverage of the Champions League group stage match between RB Leipzig and Manchester City from Saxony. The hosts started the day in 27th place in the 36-team table after two defeats, both by four goals to one, in away games against Como and Real Madrid. City begin proceedings in 12th after victories over Porto and AEK sandwiching that rip-roaring 4-2 defeat by the champions PSG at the Etihad.

City, who seemed in rude health after seven successive wins at the start of the Premier League campaign despite the guilty verdicts in the Premier League’s case against them for financial cheating, have wobbled since then, losing their last two league games. Marc Guéhi and Gigi Donnarumma are both suffering bouts of poor form, other individual errors continue to plague them and, although they are creating hatfuls of chances, they have been thwarted by a combination of imprecise finishing and the excellence of Zion Suzuki and Bart Verbruggen.

For all their travails on the road – RB Leipzig have also lost at Werder Bremen, Bayer Leverkusen and Bayern Munich – they have won all their home Bundesliga matches as well as a 1-0 victory over PSV in this competition. Their total of 22 league goals is second only to Bayern’s 27 and Antonio Nusa, a Norway team-mate of Erling Haaland, is in sparkling form flitting behind strikers Christopher Nkunku and Romulo. City, whose full-backs, if you can describe the centre-backs and midfielders who play either side of the centre-halves in that way, never look fit for purpose defensively and may well have their work cut out tonight if he drifts wide.

In a recent development, the Red Bull coaching principles, which have treated us to the dross football of Jesse Marsch, Matthias Jaissle and Ralph Hasenhüttl, all about the long pass, the central channel, counter-pressing and second balls, have a new proponent in Martín Demichelis, the forner City and Argentina defender who won the title in 2014 at the Etihad. Three years ago he led River Plate to the title in Argentina, the highlight of a coaching career also spent running Bayern’s U21s, Monterey and Mallorca.

Recent findings suggest that these two have met six times in the last five years, City winning four, most notably the 7-0 thrashing at the Etihad in 2023’s Round of 16, the year they went on to win the Treble. Leipzig’s only victory came at home five years ago in the sixth, redundant group game when City and PSG had already clinched qualification for the knockout stages.

Antoine Semenyo is City’s only absentee; Leipzig will have to do without one-cap Germany midfielder Assan Ouédraogo and former Chelsea striker Marc Guiu.

Can you tell us the answer to this quiz question?

Which player comes next in the sequence? Alexander Hleb, Robert Pires, Dennis Bergkamp, Kolo Toure, Thierry Henry, Robert Pires, Thierry Henry, Thierry Henry, Thierry Henry….

According to recent reports, we'll reveal the answer this time next week when we reach the next edition of The Pre-Match Poser – for now, here's the answer to last week's poser…Q. Only 10 managers have ever had it. Brian Clough was the first, Sir Alex Ferguson was the longest, Sean Dyche and Eddie Howe were the last Englishmen, and Mikel Arteta is one of three Arsenal managers. What are we talking about?A. The title of being the longest-serving manager in the Premier League.

Clough went into the first Prem season having been Nottingham Forest boss since the 1970s; Fergie took the title in February 1995 and held onto it until his retirement in May 2013; Eddie Howe had the title at Bournemouth before leaving, when Sean Dyche took it over; and Arteta has followed Arsene Wenger and George Graham to become the longest-serving in the Premier League today.

The release celebrates the 190th edition of the modern Oktoberfest beer festival, which began in 1810 with the royal wedding of Bavariaâs Crown Prince Ludwig (later King Ludwig I) and Princess Therese von Sachsen-Hildburghausen.

Fittingly, the 2025 kit blends football heritage with Alpine craftsmanship.

Built on a light beige base, the shirt draws inspiration from traditional Tracht garments worn during the festival, accented with deep green tones that echo the colours of Bavarian attire. The kit is completed with black shorts and socks featuring green trims, while a wider collection adds a cap, training top, button-down tracksuit jacket, and matching pants, all styled in grey with subtle green accents.

Bayern will debut the kit in their home clash against Werder Bremen on September 26.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Washington Spirit won it all in 2021 but came up just short in each of the last two finals.
  • The Kansas City Current bring plenty to the final and may just be the favorites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for the third straight time, the Washington Spirit are playing for the NWSL Championship. The No. 3 Spirit host the No. 4 Kansas City Current at Audi Field on Saturday for the biggest prize in domestic women's soccer. Kickoff is at 8 p.m. ET, and you can see it all on CBS and Paramount+.

The Washington Spirit won it all in 2021 but came up just short in each of the last two finals. This may be the day that Trinity Rodman gets her second crown.

The Kansas City Current bring plenty to the final and may just be the favorites. They're back in the massive game for the first time since 2022 after ending NJ/NY Gotham FC's title defense in the semis. Croix Bethune, who used to play for the Spirit, curled in a free-kick stunner, and Haley Hopkins won it in the 89th minute.

So who lifts the trophy? Our experts make their picks below.

Recent findings suggest that star-studded attack: This year's finalists did not have the most straightforward journeys to the NWSL Championship, but the good news for each of them is that there will be few excuses when they finally take to the pitch on Saturday. Trinity Rodman is about to cap off a career-best campaign after an injury-riddled 2025 season and will be joined by the impactful Sofia Cantore and midseason arrival Clara Luvanga, putting the Washington Spirit in as good a position as any to come out with a win that has eluded them over the last two seasons. The Current, though, are in the same boat --  they have struggled without their all-star trio, but each of Croix Bethune, Temwa Chawinga and Michelle Cooper will be available on Saturday and equally capable of turning the game in their favor.

Sources indicate that midfield battles: There's going to be a real display of veteran prowess and eager energy. Both teams have experienced players and rising stars, and it'll be a combo of chess and tug of war during the NWSL Championship. Washington Spirit's Andi Sullivan anchors most things in the middle, with Leicy Santos linking play and Melissa Bethi's recent rise in form. Even with all the changes from injuries to departures and returns from maternity leave, the Spirit are gelling at a good time in a crucial part of the pitch. They'll battle against Kansas City's Lo'eau LaBonta and Vanessa DiBernardo, two of the best in the league with longevity and finesse. Ball knowers understand that they're two players who can control a game, close and create lanes, or serve up goals and assists. Add attacking mid Croix Bethune into the mix, and Kansas City have plenty of ways to win the middle of the park. -- Sandra Herrera.

Balance: At their best, the Washington Spirit are a side who can win a game in multiple ways, and while there's plenty of star power on both sides, balance is where they win out. It's a fascinating match for both sides and one where the margins will be thin but being able to have a strong attack led by Trinity Rodman along with a buildup that Andi Sullivan keeps control of. If the Spirit can control the pace, it will be a long day for Kansas City but Croix Bethune will have ideas of her own as well. -- Chuck Booth.

Washington Spirit: The Spirit have tossed around the phrase that the third time's the charm after two empty-handed trips to the NWSL Championship and this year, it's hard not to buy the argument. Rodman is happy and healthy but she is just one part of a team that has been smartly assembled over the years and seems as cohesive as ever. -- Pardeep Cattry.

Washington Spirit: Truthfully, the pressure is on the Washington Spirit headed into this one, and that typically doesn't play out the best for teams who are the higher seed or considered favorites on paper. Kansas City will be a more than worthy opponent, but the Spirit's third time in the final comes with a long home build-up through and back to Audi Field, and any mental component needed will come with a boost from the crowd environment. -- Sandra Herrera.

Washington Spirit: Sure, this is a "neutral" venue, but being a home team in a final match will carry the Spirit at Rowdy Audi. Considering that this is the third consecutive final, fans snatched up tickets as soon as they could, assuming that the home side would be here. While all the pressure is on the Spirit and rightfully so, the team has also embraced that, and once the first goal goes in the net, this is going to turn into a party. -- Chuck Booth.

Trinity Rodman: Is this an obvious choice? Yes, yes it is, but to be fair, Rodman has earned the right to be the easy pick. She has always been key to the Spirit's success but hit a upcoming level this season, to the point that she had a very valid MVP case even if her ex-teammate Ashley Sanchez took it home instead after a record-breaking season with the North Carolina Courage. Rodman's ability to create and score chances means she's very likely to have a say on Saturday, one that could very well end the Spirit's five-year wait for another championship. -- Pardeep Cattry.

In a recent development, clara Luvanga: The last few NWSL Championship MVPs have gone to the lone goal scorer. Barbra Banda won it in 2024 for her game-winning goal, and Rose Lavelle earned it for her single title goal in 2025. If these two teams match up on the pitch as evenly as they do on paper, then it could come down to a single moment again, and Luvanga has shown she's better positioned for it with her current form. Her four goals and three assists through seven games make her an efficient threat on goal, and could finally be the difference maker for the group in their third final. -- Sandra Herrera.

Sources indicate that trinity Rodman: To win finals, you need your best players to be at their best. All eyes have been on Trinity Rodman this season after she became the highest-paid player in NWSL history, and she has delivered. Considering that the next development in her career is to become a player for the biggest moments, and capping off the final by scoring will be just the way to do it. -- Chuck Booth.

Harry Kane ankle surgery: Why Bayern Munich may not have squad depth to withstand months without star striker

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (615 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cbssports

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bayern Munich's depth was already pushed to the limit, but Friday's 1-1 draw with Koln may have broken Vincent Kompany's side.
  • "Harry Kane underwent successful surgery overnight after tearing his left ankle ligament in yesterday's home match against 1.
  • Counting down the days already ❤️‍🩹 pic.twitter.com/rpNWUxc4vW.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bayern Munich's depth was already pushed to the limit, but Friday's 1-1 draw with Koln may have broken Vincent Kompany's side. Ballon d'Or winner Harry Kane lasted only 20 minutes before exiting with what the club is calling a "syndesmosis ligament tear in his left ankle," which required surgery overnight and will keep him sidelined "for months," according to sporting director Max Eberl.

"Harry Kane underwent successful surgery overnight after tearing his left ankle ligament in yesterday's home match against 1. FC Köln. The 33-year-old will now begin his rehab," Bayern stated in a statement.

Counting down the days already ❤️‍🩹 pic.twitter.com/rpNWUxc4vW.

Losing Kane alone is a significant blow to the Bavarians after they failed to replace Nicolas Jackson when his loan ended, but the injuries didn't stop there. Michael Olise was also withdrawn at halftime and left the stadium on crutches.

This led to a match in which Bayern put only one shot on target against a side just above the relegation zone, showing this is a problem of their own creation in the transfer market. Coming into the season without a viable backup for an aging Kane would eventually hurt Bayern, and Kompany now needs to oversee a worst-case scenario. Luis Diaz and Ismael Saibari were already out with injuries, and when Kane went down, Thomas Bischof had to come in for him instead of a like-for-like striker. Even with Jamal Musiala's neurological concerns, the players they do have aren't able to perform at their best.

According to recent reports, already in an actual title race in the Bundesliga with Borussia Dortmund, these are the kinds of setbacks that can lead to a new German champion for the first time since Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24, and even they had to go undefeated to accomplish that feat, while this season could be Bayern's own undoing. They've been one of the top sides in the world when healthy, but as it is, this side will struggle in Champions League play, where they'll travel to face Lille. Precariously in 13th place in the Champions League league phase, Bayern won't fall out of the top 24 without Kane, but it could get close to something that they should be concerned about. Even missing out on the top eight and needing to play additional games is something that Bayern won't want to deal with, considering this injury crisis.

Being a backup to Kane is a thankless task, as it's hard to get game time and you're also compared to one of the best players in the world, but it's still a multifaceted failure for Bayern to not have one. Real Madrid were able to recruit post-prime players to back up Karim Benzema, and now Kylian Mbappe has a backup from the academy. There's no reason that a club of Bayern's stature shouldn't be able to do the same, but here we are in the same position they constantly find themselves in.

It has been revealed that depth complications have held Bayern back from claiming a Champions League title in recent years. Kane winning the Ballon d'Or solidified that the starting XI is more than good enough to lift Europe's most coveted club trophy, and the difference between this side and the 2020 one that won the Champions League is their lack of depth.

It's a strange situation with Musiala that isn't being handled well, with board members open to selling him, and it doesn't help the club's overall trajectory. Bayern will need to shake things up in January, but these complications began long before now, and to return to the top of the global game, they need to change the way they do things.

Latest Update: Borussia Dortmund bows to fan pressure and end Rheinmetall deal

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.
  • The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season.
  • "It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two years of fan pressure and criticism has forced Borussia Dortmund to drop a sponsorship deal with Germany's largest arms manufacturer, Rheinmetall.

The Bundesliga club will not renew its deal with Rheinmetall beyond its expiry in June 2027, at the end of this season. Dortmund chairman Carsten Cramer confirmed the news on the club's website ahead of its AGM on Sunday, which may have proved a potential flashpoint. He acknowledged that "our partnership has been controversial from the outset" but lamented the loss of income.

"It reduces our financial room for manoeuvre. We will have to reprioritize planned investments and carefully examine how we can find viable solutions.".

Though he welcomed the news, one of the leaders of the fan revolt against the partnership, Michael Schulze von Glaser, warned this is likely not the end of the road.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, "I think in the end it was a victory for the fans. But I'm also a bit skeptical about  what the future will bring us," the Dortmund fan and former head of the German Peace Society told DW. "Football fans in Germany always must be skeptical and always must watch what the club is doing.”.

Many Dortmund fans have opposed the deal — which has seen Rheinmetall's logo on advertising boards and other surfaces at locations such as Dortmund's 83,000-capacity Westfalenstadion — from its beginnings in 2024. It was estimated to be worth between €7 ($7.68 million) and €9 million per year.

According to recent reports, at the club's AGM that year, 556 of 855 members present voted against the deal in a non-binding vote. There were 247 votes in favour, with 52 abstentions. This, stated Cramer, informed the eventual outcome.

In a recent development, rheinmetall sells arms mostly to Germany, Ukraine and NATO but fans and critics feel that platforming any arms manufacturer goes against the club's statement of its core values. In that, Dortmund states its desire for "a club and a society that operate free of racism, anti-Semitism, LGBTQIA+ hostility, sexism, violence and discrimination.".

To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio.

It has always been clear, remarked Schulze von Glaser, that this deal did not chime with that.

Industry observers note that "In the end, they kill people. They are for war," he said of Rheinmetall. "The slogan of Borussia Dortmund is true love (Echte Liebe). But for me and many others, our love ends there…. I know some fans who have put fan merchandise in the trash because they were so shocked.”.

In the Q and A on the club's website, Cramer remarked he was still a "personal advocate" of the deal but that Dortmund's commitment to the 50+1 model, which means German clubs are majority controlled by the members, meant they had to listen to fan voices. But he also warned that Rheinmetall must be an "absolute exception and an isolated case.".

That set off some alarm bells for Schulze von Glaser.

"It's a bit concerning that there are constantly these attacks on professional football — a new sponsorship, investment deals," he noted.

Indeed, Dortmund's climbdown is not the first of its kind in Germany's top flight. Last year, after fan and media pressure, Bayern Munich ended its commercial deal with the tourism arm of the Rwandan government before its conclusion.

According to recent reports, fans had objected to the promotion of Rwanda, which many felt sought to divert attention from its poor human rights record and actions in the war with DR Congo, through sporting partnerships. Two years earlier, Bayern withdrew from a similarly controversial deal with Qatar Airways.

Elsewhere in the league, Werder Bremen fans objected to their long time shirt sponsor, Wiesenhof. Many supporters took glitch with the factory farming practices  of Germany's largest poultry producer. Though it was not given as a direct reason for the end of a shirt sponsorship deal in 2023, it likely played a part.

According to recent reports, union Berlin fans have also made their voices heard. When the club signed a fresh shirt-sponsorship deal with Luxembourg real estate company, Aroundtown, upon promotion to the top flight in 2019, many fans were frustrated at the tie up in a city where rent prices were skyrocketing.

"It's a problem for a lot of people," fan Sven Dobberstein told DW at the time.

In a recent development, "We have to try to find a way between commercialization and what we have at the moment. It isn't easy.".

It has been revealed that striking that balance can often be a source of tension for Bundesliga clubs. 50+1 ensures fans have a voice, preventing rich owners, or nation states, from taking control as they do in England's lucrative Premier League or in France or Spain. Indeed fan protests have also stopped the league signing a €1billion private equity partner and seen Monday night matches scrapped. For Schulze von Glaser, this needs to be protected.

"In Germany, the fan culture has an impact," he mentioned.

”If there is something bad or terrible happening in your club and in the Bundesliga, there are the organized fans and they can have an impact if they want, if they stand together and, yes, they can stop the Rheinmetall deal.".

Additional reporting by: Emmie Eernisse.

Leeds expose Chelsea's unresolved defensive problems as Xabi Alonso's crew yet to find footing

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that LONDON -- This was supposed to be the year, the time when Chelsea grew up and a proper manager started extracting consistent performances from a squad whose much-vaunted talent is too rarely expressed in results form.
  • It has been revealed that once more, however, that is threatening to be a standard beyond Chelsea.
  • In a recent development, and Alonso has tried a lot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that LONDON -- This was supposed to be the year, the time when Chelsea grew up and a proper manager started extracting consistent performances from a squad whose much-vaunted talent is too rarely expressed in results form. In this most in-flux of Premier League seasons, Xabi Alonso still might leave her with something. It is not going to take particular excellence for a club like this to achieve the bare minimum of Champions League qualification. Adequacy might do it.

It has been revealed that once more, however, that is threatening to be a standard beyond Chelsea. This 4-1 defeat at home to old rivals Leeds has them squeezed into the Premier League's middle ground, those above them very visible proof of how much more can be done with less. There is nothing false about that position. Since the last weeks of summer, Alonso's team have given up so much at the back that their likeliest route to success seemed to be supernova seasons from all three of Morgan Rogers, Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro. Nothing else would paper over the cracks in the defense.

In a recent development, and Alonso has tried a lot. Right backs in midfield, center backs as nominal left wing backs that are actually auxiliary central midfielders, switching the right wing back to center forward: in isolation, you could make a case for so many of these adjustments. When the performances are so inconsistent, why not change the XI every game? Alonso's success at Bayer Leverkusen, coupled with the inquisitive footballing mind that made the player so beloved of elite coaches, have earned him the right to experiment.

Every change, however, begs the question of what the foundations underlying all this are. Those ought to have shone through this afternoon. Alonso's was as straightforward an XI as he has named. Estevao, Palmer and Rogers off an orthodox center forward, Moises Caicedo running the double pivot and an orthodox back four in front of Emiliano Martinez. This looked like a team intent on playing its way.

Sources indicate that instead, they had Leeds' game foisted upon them. That might have been different if they had not lost Caicedo. He seemed to have a handle on the game before colliding with James Justin as both competed for a high ball. Those often seemed like the only sort up for grabs today; even when Chelsea played well, they were playing the sort of game Leeds wanted. This wasn't quite the rapid attacking up the gut with which Xabi Alonso charmed the Premier League early in this season. It was bypass the press-ball, get it straight up to the final third and see what comes of it.

It can work. Justin, exemplary as a man-marker without the ball and roving agent of chaos in the Chelsea half, cleared a goal kick straight into the back of Morgan Rogers. He moved swiftly up the Leeds gut, his pass to Emmanuel Emegha delivered at just the right moment for the Premier League debutant to slam in the opener. It was perhaps the only moment of clinical execution from the Blues.

They needed so many more. After all, this is a team that fails to meet the standards in so many aspects of defending. They press like a newly promoted team. They always seem to name one defender who can be picked on in the duels (starting left back Pep Charravia ranks 101st of 102 defenders for duel success over 300-plus Premier League minutes). Midfielders routinely abandon runners. When Caicedo left this game the feint thread holding the team together was cut.

Industry observers note that no one had the composure to deal with the bouncing ball moments after Emegha's opener, Noah Okafor free to move into the box and shoot low through a crowd of legs. No one seemed truly live to the danger for Okafor's second, thundered into the roof of the net when Chelsea could not repel pressure down their right. Between that a contentious penalty, Jayden Bogle's long-range effort striking Rogers right in the grey area between sleeve and arm. If that hadn't been the moment when Chelsea caved, another would have come along.

Sources indicate that "Leeds believed more than us," Alonso admitted. "We didn't show a good enough reaction." The quick one-two punch had been more than enough to send Chelsea heads to the floor.

Industry observers note that A two-goal deficit ought not to be beyond their reach, but the final 32 minutes saw them outshot seven to six with fewer passes completed into the penalty area. Palmer's most notable action of this game was to row with Joao Pedro as he made his way down the tunnel. Nothing he could have done would have overcome the problems Chelsea made for themselves at the other end. It really wouldn't hurt, though if he did more than nothing.

These feel like problems unresolved by a manager who was supposed to be the savior. Eleven Premier League games is not a lot to turn the tide but it is enough to give us a sense of who this team are. The answer is a team whose early scoring streak covered for a below-average attack (1.25 non-penalty expected goals per game, 14th in the Premier League) and a below-average defense (1.44 non-penalty expected goals allowed per game, 15th in the Premier League). The game state-warping impact of scoring with your first shot can only mitigate so much.

Is it time for a conversation about Alonso and pressure? If so it has to be caveated by the unity and purpose he fostered at Bayer Leverkusen, qualities this dressing room sorely needs. He might not have corralled the superstars at Real Madrid but the press and possession system he forged could have achieved great things given time. Stitching together a version of this Chelsea, overloaded with number 10s and underpowered defensive players, that suits the more direct and chaotic Premier League was always going to be a coaching challenge.

Sources indicate that and of course this is not the Roman Abramovich era. Swapping out coaches is not a silver bullet for perennial trophy contenders but instead the modus operandi of an ownership group that are the most serious problem at Stamford Bridge. Someone is going to have to be afforded time to corral this squad or indeed tear it down and start again. Doing that is going to be a club-wide effort, including fans. Few of them hung around to wave off a side who had allowed old rivals Leeds a first win at Stamford Bridge since 1999, the same side who had let Tottenham break the habit of a lifetime last month.

According to recent reports, the vibes are bad. The performances might be worse. This brand newly introduced start is feeling all too familiar.
